input:
This staffing review examines the position in a dispatch office that employs 14 full-time staff, where overtime working currently accounts for 15% of paid hours, based on the figures for last year. One option under consideration is to replace half of this overtime with one additional hire, which would cost $91k per year on a fully loaded basis. At first glance, this appears to offer an attractive opportunity to reduce the burden of overtime working and to provide a more sustainable staffing model for the office going forward.

However, it is important to note that the overtime in question is not spread evenly throughout the year. Instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, which means that for substantial parts of the year the office operates comfortably within its normal staffing levels. A new hire, by contrast, is paid for the full year, regardless of whether the additional capacity is actually required at any given time. This represents a significant consideration, since the $91k annual cost is committed in full from the moment the appointment is made.

Nevertheless, there are also important benefits to be weighed in the balance. Overtime at the seasonal peaks is worked by members of staff who are already carrying a full schedule, and the peak periods are precisely the times at which the dispatch office can least afford errors or unexpected absences. Reducing the overtime burden at these critical times could therefore deliver meaningful improvements in resilience and service quality. On balance, the review concludes that the proposal merits serious consideration, while recognising that the present overtime level would only be partially addressed, since half of the overtime would remain in place even after the additional hire has been appointed and has settled into the role.
target:
The dispatch office carries overtime at 15% of paid hours with a staff of 14 full-time employees, and the review's proposal is to replace half of that overtime with one additional hire at $91k per year, fully loaded. The comparison the proposal rests on is between a recurring overtime bill concentrated in part of the year and a salary committed for the whole of it.

Overtime at this level is not spread evenly across the year. It is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and outside those peaks the office works within its staffed hours. A hire is paid for the full year, including the months in which the overtime does not arise. The $91k therefore buys cover at the peaks and spare capacity between them, and the case for the hire depends on whether the peak cover alone justifies a full-year cost.

Against that, overtime at the peaks is worked by staff who are already carrying a full schedule, and the peak is exactly the period at which the dispatch office can least absorb error or absence. Replacing half the overtime halves the peak load carried as extra hours; the remaining half stays as overtime, so the proposal reduces peak overtime rather than removing it. The hire also converts a variable cost into a fixed one: the overtime bill falls when volumes fall, and the salary does not.

The review's judgement is that the exchange is worth making on the peak evidence, with the limit stated plainly: the saving claim extends only to the half of overtime replaced, the cost is committed in full from the appointment date, and in a year without the seasonal peaks the hire is a cost carried against no overtime saving. On that basis the office gains cover where its risk is concentrated, at a fixed cost whose size is known in advance, and gives up flexibility it currently holds in the troughs between peaks.
